primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'L_{pf}': 'dimensionless leverage score from paired flip', 'L_{nf}': 'dimensionless leverage score from naive filter'}

primitives.breakdown_regime: When teams' rating paths diverge due to simulation dynamics, naive filters inflate leverage values.

primitives.name: Dynamic Rating Contamination
primitives.verbatim_quote: Season sims whose team ratings update inside the simulation (Elo-style, K = 1.75 points, logistic scale 5.5) contaminate outcome-filtered leverage: filtering on "team won" also selects the sims where the team's rating path drifted up.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'R(t)': 'team rating at time t during simulation', 'W': 'win event indicator'}
primitives.assumptions: Rating updates occur dynamically based on match outcomes; filtering on win condition includes upward-drift simulations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Filtering on outcome alone leads to spurious leverage when rating trajectories are correlated with wins.

layer2.mapping: Contamination arises from the kernel of rating evolution being conflated with outcome selection, distorting empirical estimates of leverage.
layer2.telemetry: Standard deviation of rating changes among winning simulations vs. non-winning simulations.

primitives.name: Inflation Factor
primitives.verbatim_quote: Timo measured the inflation at 1.3-1.6x per team on his real Week 7 setup.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'I': 'inflation factor (1.3–1.6)', 'L_{nf}': 'leverage under naive filter', 'L_{pf}': 'leverage under paired flip'}
primitives.assumptions: Measured in real-world NFL simulations with fixed parameters; reflects ratio of inflated to true leverage.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Inflation occurs when dynamic ratings are used in outcome-based filtering without correction.

layer2.mapping: Inflation factor quantifies how much naive leverage overestimates true leverage due to rating-path correlation.
layer2.telemetry: Ratio I = L_nf / L_pf averaged across all teams in a given week.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that outcome-filtered leverage in dynamic Elo simulations suffers from a systematic bias caused by rating path correlation. When a team wins, its rating may have drifted upward due to prior games, which inflates the perceived leverage of that win. The paired-flip method addresses this by isolating the impact of a single game’s outcome while holding all other ratings constant. This creates a clean counterfactual where only the focal game changes, removing the confounding effect of rating drift. The inflation factor (1.3–1.6x) demonstrates the magnitude of this artifact in practice. In GSI, this manifests as a need for conformal prediction layers that account for such biases in probabilistic forecasting. In GSE, it necessitates state transitions that preserve rating invariance under outcome filtering. The dual nature of the problem—bias from dynamic updating versus control from static reference—is resolved through the paired flip, which acts as a conservative estimator bracketing the true effect between frozen and naive approaches.
